title: The Unwritten Letter
premise: In the winter of 1946, Freya Galloway carries diplomatic pouches for the collapsing Republic of Velden, a courier trusted with sealed orders she is never meant to read. When a stranger named Tomas Reiner arrives bearing a letter in the handwriting of her brother Anders — officially dead for two years — she discovers the republic's new masters falsified his death to bury evidence of a massacre ordered at the highest level. Pursued by intelligence officers determined to erase the paper trail, Freya and Tomas race across a fractured country to place the true record before an international tribunal before the year ends and the victors' historians seal the archive. The book ends with Freya testifying, Anders's letter entered into the record, and her choosing exile with Tomas over a decorated lie at home.
about_author: Dominic Underhill is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing displaced-persons records in postwar Europe. He writes historical fiction about the small, carryable objects — letters, keys, ledgers — through which ordinary people hold power to account.

chapters.title: The Weight of Sealed Things
chapters.summary: Freya Galloway, POV. In the republic's final weeks, Freya runs dispatches through checkpoints, measuring her life in what fits in a courier satchel. She learns her brother Anders, a government clerk, is officially dead. The beat is quiet dread: the state that employs her has begun lying to her personally.

chapters.title: Handwriting for the Dead
chapters.summary: Freya, POV. A stranger, Tomas Reiner, intercepts her at a rail depot and shows her a letter in Anders's unmistakable hand, dated three months after his reported death. Freya's grief curdles into suspicion. The emotional beat is vertigo — the ground of the official record giving way beneath her.

chapters.title: The Archive Burns on Schedule
chapters.summary: Tomas, POV. Tomas, a former records officer turned smuggler of documents, explains that Anders discovered falsified casualty ledgers from the Karsten Valley operation and went into hiding with the originals. Freya refuses to believe the republic she serves is guilty. The beat is friction between belief and evidence.

chapters.title: Orders Come in Duplicate
chapters.summary: Freya, POV. Her ministry hands her a sealed pouch with instructions to destroy its duplicate en route. Instead she opens it: an order authorizing 'disposition' of surviving valley witnesses. The beat is a point of no return crossed quietly, in an ordinary train compartment.

chapters.title: The Man Who Signs as Nobody
chapters.summary: Tomas, POV. Tomas reveals he was the officer ordered to kill Anders and chose to fake the death instead, keeping the letter as insurance. Freya must decide whether a confessed executioner can be trusted. The beat is wary, charged alliance — the first flicker of something beyond necessity between them.

chapters.title: Karsten Valley, in Winter
chapters.summary: Freya, POV. They travel to the valley, finding a village of survivors who recognize Freya's ministry insignia and spit at it. An old woman gives Freya her own copy of a ledger page. The beat is shame made physical; belonging to the state now costs her belonging anywhere.

chapters.title: The Historian's Apprentice
chapters.summary: New character Ilse Brandt, POV. Ilse, a young archivist for the incoming victors' commission, is ordered to 'curate' the Karsten file — meaning sanitize it. She hesitates over an anomaly: two versions of one ledger. The beat is a mirror to Freya; another woman choosing what the record will say.

chapters.title: What the Satchel Carries
chapters.summary: Freya, POV. Pursued by Major Kessler of the intelligence directorate, Freya and Tomas split the documents between them so neither carries the whole truth. In a safehouse they nearly part ways; instead they admit, obliquely, that they have stopped thinking of the mission as duty alone. The beat is love surfacing under pressure.

chapters.title: Kessler's Courtesy
chapters.summary: Kessler, POV. Kessler, urbane and genuinely convinced he is saving the nation from another civil war, offers Freya amnesty and a promotion to return the pouches. He shows her a photograph of her mother's address — a threat wrapped in kindness. The beat is corruption wearing a reasonable face.

chapters.title: The Ferry at Vosk
chapters.summary: Tomas, POV. A betrayal by a trusted contact strands them; Tomas takes a bullet in the shoulder getting Freya and the ledgers onto a ferry. Freya digs the bullet out herself. The beat is intimacy forced by crisis — she saves the man who saved the truth.

chapters.title: A Republic's Last Communique
chapters.summary: Freya, POV. The republic formally dissolves; Freya's commission, her identity papers, her whole framework of duty expires by decree. She is, officially, no one. The beat is liberation and terror in the same breath: without duty, what is she loyal to?

chapters.title: Ilse Opens the Wrong Drawer
chapters.summary: Ilse, POV. Ilse finds the original casualty ledgers misfiled — deliberately — and realizes her superiors are building a false archive in parallel. She copies the discrepancy and mails it to a tribunal address she is not authorized to contact. The beat is a small act of enormous courage.

chapters.title: The Border That Moves
chapters.summary: Freya, POV. The tribunal's jurisdiction boundary is redrawn overnight, putting their destination outside protection. They must cross into the tribunal zone before the new map takes effect in six days. The beat is a ticking clock made literal, geography itself turning hostile.

chapters.title: Hostage to the Ledger
chapters.summary: Kessler, POV. Kessler captures Anders — alive, worn, unbroken — and offers to trade him for the documents. Freya must weigh her brother against the record. The beat is the book's cruelest choice, and Freya, agonized, refuses to trade the truth for love of family.

chapters.title: Anders, in Person
chapters.summary: Anders, POV. Anders, escaped with Ilse's help, reaches Freya and explains why he let the world believe him dead: a living witness can be silenced; a dead man's documents cannot. He forgives Freya for her refusal. The beat is reconciliation — family restored on the far side of sacrifice.

chapters.title: The Night Before the Map
chapters.summary: Freya, POV. On the eve of the crossing, in a barn, Freya and Tomas finally speak plainly of what they are to each other, and of what they will lose if they fail. The beat is stillness before the storm; the love declared precisely because tomorrow may cancel it.

chapters.title: Crossing at First Light
chapters.summary: Tomas, POV. The border crossing goes wrong; Kessler's men intercept. In the firefight, Tomas is gravely wounded shielding the satchel, and Ilse arrives with the tribunal escort she summoned. The beat is chaos resolving into salvation — the small acts of many converging.

chapters.title: Kessler's Last Argument
chapters.summary: Freya, POV. Cornered, Kessler makes his final case: the massacre prevented a worse war, and history will thank whoever writes it. Freya answers that history thanks no one; it only records. Kessler, defeated not by force but by the arriving tribunal officers, stands down. The beat is the theme stated and won.

chapters.title: On the Record
chapters.summary: Freya, POV. In the tribunal chamber, Freya testifies, and Anders's letter — read aloud, entered as exhibit — becomes the hinge of the Karsten inquiry. Ilse's parallel ledger discrepancy corroborates everything. The beat is catharsis: the truth, at last, uncarryable, unkillable, public.

chapters.title: The Historians Arrive
chapters.summary: Ilse, POV. The victors' commission attempts to bury the tribunal findings anyway; Ilse leaks the full file to three foreign newspapers simultaneously, making suppression impossible. She loses her post and gains her conscience. The beat is the theme completed — power corrupts, but paper outlasts it.

chapters.title: What Can Be Carried
chapters.summary: Freya, POV. Offered reinstatement and honors by the successor state if she recants, Freya declines. She and Tomas, with Anders, board a westbound train with one satchel between them: the original letter. The beat is resolution — she chooses belonging to people over belonging to power.

chapters.title: The Unwritten Letter
chapters.summary: Freya, POV, years later. In exile, Freya begins a letter to the old woman of Karsten Valley and cannot finish it — no words are adequate, so instead she sends the published tribunal transcript with a single line enclosed. The final beat: some truths can be carried after all, once they are shared.
